mentions.quote: for cows and land, by the king's order in market places
mentions.role: authority setting commodity prices

mentions.quote: When the king grants a field, he should have it demarcated
mentions.role: grantor of land with demarcation duty

mentions.quote: so the king should establish it with justice for the two villages
mentions.role: arbiter of boundary disputes

mentions.quote: all of them should be punished separately by the king with the middle amercement
mentions.role: punisher of false witnesses

mentions.quote: The king should make the boundary of ten villages, a hundred villages, or a thousand villages
mentions.role: administrative boundary-setter

mentions.quote: the king should pour heated oil into his mouth and ears
mentions.role: enforcer of caste-based speech laws

mentions.quote: by a king who desires the welfare of the world, violent criminals … should not be released
mentions.role: protector of public order

mentions.quote: The king who, out of greed or fear, does not kill wrongdoers, his kingdom becomes agitated
mentions.role: responsible for social order through punishment

entities.description: The king is the supreme judicial and administrative authority whose duty is to set prices, demarcate land, punish criminals, and maintain social order.
entities.justification: The king appears repeatedly as the central enforcer of legal norms across sale, boundary, assault, theft, and homicide sections throughout this window.

mentions.quote: overseen by men learned in the four Vedas
mentions.role: Veda-learned overseers of land demarcation

mentions.quote: He should make a Brahmin swear by truth
mentions.role: witness sworn by truth in boundary disputes

mentions.quote: For one who gives a religious instruction unrighteously to Brahmins, the king should pour heated oil into his mouth and ears
mentions.role: protected class; wronging them incurs severe punishment

mentions.quote: For defaming a Kshatriya, the fine for a Brahmin is fifty
mentions.role: liable party in inter-caste defamation fines

mentions.quote: In an assault on one devoid of good qualities, a Brahmin is not at fault
mentions.role: exempted from punishment when assaulting the unworthy

mentions.quote: one who gives religious instruction accompanied by citations from the Veda, but insults Brahmins, is to be punished by the cutting out of his tongue
mentions.role: protected from insult under severe penalty

mentions.quote: For transgressing against a Brahmin … he should be killed
mentions.role: highest-status victim class requiring capital punishment for transgressors

mentions.quote: With whatever limb a Shudra strikes one of the twice-born in anger, that [limb] must be cut off
mentions.role: protected class; assaults by lower castes require amputation

mentions.quote: The killing of an ātatāyin, a Brahmin, or a sacrificial animal in a righteous battle
mentions.role: specially proscribed killing in Kali Yuga

mentions.quote: A thief who is of good conduct and learned in the Veda is to be tormented in prison for a long time
mentions.role: Veda-learned criminal accorded mitigated but prolonged punishment

entities.description: Brahmins are the priestly social class who are specially protected from insult and assault, serve as sworn witnesses, and whose killing or defaming incurs the heaviest legal penalties.
entities.justification: Brahmins appear throughout the assault, defamation, theft, and heinous crime sections as the highest-status protected group whose harm by lower castes triggers graduated punishment.

mentions.quote: a Kshatriya by his vehicle and weapons
mentions.role: sworn by symbols of martial honor in boundary disputes

mentions.quote: For defaming a Kshatriya, the fine for a Brahmin is fifty
mentions.role: subject of inter-caste defamation fine schedule

mentions.quote: For a Vaishya insulting a Kshatriya, a fine of one hundred should be imposed
mentions.role: protected from insult by Vaishya with heavy fine

mentions.quote: For a Kshatriya insulting a Shudra, the fine is twenty-five
mentions.role: fined for insulting Shudra, but at lower rate

entities.description: Kshatriyas are the warrior-ruling social class who are sworn by their martial symbols and occupy the second rank in the caste-based fine schedule for verbal assault.
entities.justification: The Kshatriya appears in the verbal and physical assault sections as a mid-tier caste whose insults and receipt of insults carry graduated fines relative to Brahmins and Vaishyas.

mentions.quote: for a Vaishya, likewise twenty-five
mentions.role: subject of inter-caste defamation fine schedule

mentions.quote: A Kshatriya insulting a Vaishya deserves half that punishment
mentions.role: receives lighter punishment when insulted by Kshatriya

mentions.quote: A Shudra insulting a Vaishya should be made to pay the first amercement
mentions.role: protected from Shudra insult at first-amercement level

entities.description: Vaishyas are the merchant-farmer social class occupying the third rank in the varna hierarchy, subject to a graduated fine schedule for inter-caste verbal and physical assaults.
entities.justification: Vaishyas appear in the verbal assault section as one of four ranked castes with specific fines calibrated to the direction of the insult.

mentions.quote: If a Shudra is the guide, having adorned him with the insignia of a eunuch, having smeared his face with the ash of a corpse
mentions.role: subjected to ritual humiliation if serving as boundary guide

mentions.quote: for a Shudra, twelve and a half
mentions.role: lowest fine-receipt tier in defamation schedule

mentions.quote: This fine is ordained for a good Shudra who is not at fault
mentions.role: good-conduct Shudra protected from unprovoked insult

mentions.quote: A Shudra insulting a Vaishya should be made to pay the first amercement; For insulting a Kshatriya, the middle; and for a Brahmin, the highest amercement
mentions.role: subject to escalating fines for insulting higher castes

mentions.quote: With whatever limb a Shudra strikes one of the twice-born in anger, that [limb] must be cut off
mentions.role: faces amputation for physically assaulting twice-born

entities.description: Shudras are the lowest varna whose legal disabilities include ritual humiliation when serving as boundary guides and harsh amputative punishments for assaulting higher castes.
entities.justification: Shudras appear across boundary demarcation, verbal assault, and physical assault sections as the legally most disadvantaged varna facing the harshest graduated penalties.

mentions.quote: Though stated by Manu, niyoga was forbidden by him himself
mentions.role: earlier lawgiver whose ruling on levirate is cited and then qualified

entities.description: Manu is the ancient lawgiver whose text is cited as a prior authority on the practice of niyoga (levirate), which Bṛhaspati then supersedes by declaring it obsolete.
entities.justification: Manu is named as the source of the niyoga rule that Bṛhaspati explicitly revokes due to the degenerate conditions of the Kali Yuga.

mentions.quote: The killing of an ātatāyin, a Brahmin, or a sacrificial animal in a righteous battle
mentions.role: one of three specially regulated killing categories

mentions.quote: In killing an ātatāyin, the killer does not incur any sin
mentions.role: legitimate target of lethal force without sin

mentions.quote: He who does not kill an ātatāyin of high rank … obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice
mentions.role: one whose killing, even if high-ranked, earns great merit

mentions.quote: He who kills an ātatāyin who is learned in the Veda and born in a good family … does not become a slayer of an embryo
mentions.role: even a Veda-learned ātatāyin may be killed without sin

mentions.quote: one who kills an ātatāyin … is not punished
mentions.role: exempt from legal punishment for defensive killing

entities.description: An ātatāyin is a person who initiates extreme aggression (arson, poisoning, etc.) and whose killing is legally and morally permitted without incurring sin or punishment.
entities.justification: The ātatāyin is a legally defined aggressor-category appearing in the heinous crime section as the paradigm case for justified homicide.

mentions.quote: The wise say that these dharmas are to be avoided in the Kali Yuga
mentions.role: the degenerate age in which certain killing-norms are suspended

mentions.quote: In the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas, a decline in the power of men has been ordained
mentions.role: era of diminished human capacity justifying stricter legal restrictions

entities.description: The Kali Yuga is the current degenerate cosmic age invoked to justify stricter or modified legal rules, including the prohibition of niyoga and avoidance of certain killing norms.
entities.justification: The Kali Yuga is explicitly cited twice in this window as the cosmological justification for departing from prior dharmaśāstra rulings.

mentions.quote: Men in the Kṛta and Tretā Yugas were endowed with austerity and knowledge. In the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas, a decline in the power of men has been ordained
mentions.role: earlier cosmic ages of superior human capacity contrasted with the present

entities.description: The Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara Yugas are the three prior cosmic ages when men possessed greater austerity and knowledge, making stricter practices like niyoga feasible.
entities.justification: These ages are invoked to contrast ideal with degraded human capacities, providing the cosmological basis for Bṛhaspati's legal modifications.

mentions.quote: overseen by men learned in the four Vedas
mentions.role: credential qualifying overseers of boundary demarcation

mentions.quote: one who gives religious instruction accompanied by citations from the Veda, but insults Brahmins
mentions.role: authoritative text whose citation during instruction does not excuse insult

mentions.quote: A thief who is of good conduct and learned in the Veda is to be tormented in prison for a long time
mentions.role: Vedic learning mitigates but does not eliminate criminal punishment

mentions.quote: ātatāyin of high rank, endowed with good conduct and Vedic learning
mentions.role: Vedic learning does not protect an aggressor from justified killing

mentions.quote: an ātatāyin who is learned in the Veda
mentions.role: Vedic learning irrelevant to legality of killing an ātatāyin

entities.description: The Veda is the sacred scriptural corpus whose mastery confers social prestige and legal standing, though it neither exempts criminals from punishment nor protects aggressors from lethal force.
entities.justification: The Veda appears as a measure of qualification and social status across boundary, verbal assault, theft, and homicide sections, consistently invoked but never as an absolute shield.

mentions.quote: #### 1.25.3 The Prohibition of niyoga
mentions.role: section heading identifying niyoga as the topic of legal prohibition

mentions.quote: Though stated by Manu, niyoga was forbidden by him himself. Due to the decline of the age, it is impossible for all to perform it according to the rule
mentions.role: practice declared forbidden due to Kali Yuga conditions

entities.description: Niyoga is the levirate practice by which a widow may produce offspring with a designated man; Bṛhaspati forbids it as unperformable in the Kali Yuga despite Manu's original allowance.
entities.justification: Niyoga receives its own dedicated subsection and is explicitly cited as Manu's ruling that Bṛhaspati overrides due to the cosmological decline of the present age.

mentions.quote: Having received saudāyika wealth, independence is desired for women, because it was given by them for kindness, as a gift
mentions.role: woman's independent wealth given as a gift of affection

entities.description: Saudāyika is a woman's personal property received as gifts from kin, over which she has independent disposal rights.
entities.justification: Saudāyika is named as a legal category of women's property in the inheritance section, distinct from jointly-held family property.

themes.topic: Graduated punishment calibrated to caste rank

mentions.quote: For defaming a Kshatriya, the fine for a Brahmin is fifty; for a Vaishya, likewise twenty-five; for a Shudra, twelve and a half
A Shudra insulting a Vaishya should be made to pay the first amercement. For insulting a Kshatriya, the middle; and for a Brahmin, the highest amercement
With whatever limb a Shudra strikes one of the twice-born in anger, that [limb] must be cut off

themes.justification: Every assault, insult, and theft section in this window calibrates fines and bodily punishments according to the caste of both perpetrator and victim, making varna-graduated punishment the structural backbone of the entire law of wrongs.

themes.topic: King's dual role as administrator and judge

mentions.quote: When the king grants a field, he should have it demarcated
so the king should establish it with justice for the two villages
The king who, out of greed or fear, does not kill wrongdoers, his kingdom becomes agitated, and he is deprived of his realm
by a king who desires the welfare of the world, violent criminals … should not be released

themes.justification: The king figures simultaneously as land-granter, boundary-arbiter, punisher of thieves and killers, and guarantor of social order, revealing kingship as both executive and judicial office throughout this window.

mentions.quote: the determination of the boundary line must be made, marked by public and secret signs
the determination of the boundary in a dispute would be by the witnesses
Sworn by their own oaths, they should state the decision on the boundary
One who is cleared by ordeals is pure; one who is not cleared deserves death

themes.justification: The text moves through a ranked evidentiary sequence—boundary signs, witnesses, oaths, and finally ordeals—reflecting a coherent procedural hierarchy for resolving disputes when lower-level proof fails.

themes.topic: Justified homicide and the ethics of killing

mentions.quote: In killing an ātatāyin, the killer does not incur any sin
He who does not kill an ātatāyin of high rank … obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice
Where the death of one evil-doer brings well-being to many, his execution is a meritorious act

themes.justification: Multiple verses construct a positive duty to kill in defined circumstances, framing certain killings as not only blameless but meritorious, which is a distinctive strand of legal-ethical reasoning in this window.

mentions.quote: What is sold by one who is intoxicated or insane, for a low price or out of fear, by one who is not independent or by a minor
An exchange made by the intoxicated, foolish, ignorant, afflicted, or deluded, and whatever has an improper price, all that is condemned
What was given to another out of satisfaction does not attain validity

themes.justification: The sale and boundary sections articulate a doctrine of legal incapacity whereby transactions by persons lacking full agency—due to intoxication, insanity, minority, or coercion—are void or voidable.

themes.topic: Women's legal status, guardian duties, and marital obligations

mentions.quote: A woman must be restrained from even the slightest attachments by her own kinsmen. She must be guarded day and night by her husband
A father who does not give his daughter in marriage at the proper time, a husband who does not approach his wife during her fertile period
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice. And prosperity, pure progeny, and fruitful rites will result
The wife is remembered as half the body, equal in the fruit of merit and demerit

themes.justification: The window contains a dedicated section on regulating women's conduct that combines prescriptions for male guardianship with idealized statements of wifely virtue and reciprocal honor, reflecting the text's dual patriarchal and protective stance.

themes.topic: Temporal degeneration and the revision of prior legal rules

mentions.quote: Though stated by Manu, niyoga was forbidden by him himself. Due to the decline of the age, it is impossible for all to perform it according to the rule
Men in the Kṛta and Tretā Yugas were endowed with austerity and knowledge. In the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas, a decline in the power of men has been ordained
The wise say that these dharmas are to be avoided in the Kali Yuga

themes.justification: Bṛhaspati uses the yuga-decline framework as an explicit jurisprudential tool to override earlier authorities (Manu) and suspend certain dharmas, demonstrating how cosmological time-theory functions as a source of legal revision.

mentions.quote: In ancestral property, a house or field, the father and sons are equal sharers. In the father's self-acquired property, the father is superior
having given a preferential share to the eldest, they are equal sharers in the remainder
For unmarried daughters, a fourth part is desired. For the sons, three parts

themes.justification: The final section of the window is devoted to elaborate rules on property partition, covering ancestral versus self-acquired wealth, birth-order preferences, and the shares of daughters and widows.

themes.topic: Secret and public signs as legal proof

mentions.quote: Imperishable things, which are naturally not subject to decay: tanks, wells, ponds, sacred monuments, gardens, and temples
other things which the earth does not consume, and other hidden things, one should make as boundary signs
Dried cow-dung, bones, chaff, charcoal, pebbles, stones, potsherds, sand, bricks, cow-hair, cotton seeds, bones, and ash

themes.justification: The distinction between public boundary markers (trees, wells) and secret buried markers (charcoal, bones in pots) implies a developed legal epistemology distinguishing communally observable proof from privately planted evidence.

citations.quote: Though stated by Manu, niyoga was forbidden by him himself. Due to the decline of the age, it is impossible for all to perform it according to the rule
citations.justification: Bṛhaspati explicitly names Manu as the prior authority on niyoga and then overrides Manu's ruling by appealing to the conditions of the Kali Yuga, making this a refutation-by-supersession.
